doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

title: Learning jazz without teachers: Bermuda practice, a fake book, melody playing
summary: Roy Marsh refused to teach him; he practised daily in Bermuda, learned tunes from a fake book and favours melody.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Yeah. You know you’ve had an interesting combination of running into people that were tough on you, and some people who sort of very serendipitously helped you out. Yeah. The part about absorbing jazz in your playing, was it mostly through listening to records?

Nobody would teach me. The only person that was playing vibes then was a man called Roy Marsh. He was working with one of these big bands. It was Eric Winstone’s big band, and three or four of the guys in the band, they came to the theater to play, and three or four of them came down to hear me play at this little ballroom where I was working in the small group and playing vibes on the side. And I asked Roy Marsh if he would teach me then and he said no, he wouldn’t teach me. So I had to make my own way. And I really wasn’t a professional caliber until I spent every day practicing in Bermuda, all the time I was there. And I formed a trio there with a couple of the local guys, African- American kids. And we had a very nice trio and so that was a good experience. And the guy let me play the odd number in the band that I was playing for the dancing. In those days, in 1950, ’51, in Bermuda, in the winter, you had to come to the ballroom to dance in a dinner jacket. And the ladies had to wear long dresses. Yeah it was very formal. But it was a good experience. I enjoyed it. It was seven nights a week for eighteen months. No night off. And on Sunday we had to do a concert. So I’d always do a vibraphone solo, you know. So that helped me develop.
If someone asked you, if they came up and said, “Can you play ‘These Foolish Things’” for instance, and you didn’t know it but you said, I better learn that song, how did you go about it back then?

I would learn the melody and then I got a fake book. Some guy on a boat, who was an American fellow, had this fake book and I bought it. It was a good fake book, just elementary changes, but it gave me the direction. And then I kept, you know I would pick up this lick and that lick. And I probably played a lot of melody more than jazz. I mean I always liked playing melody.

Yeah. I made a beautiful record with strings some years ago, Rick Wilkins the great arranger that used to arrange for the Boss Brass, did the arrangements for me. And it really was a nice record. And it was at the time when we would get airplay on the FM stations, so it got a lot of play.
